interest: Imperial-family dockets, 1930–37, and Grew's January 1938 report on the Allison assault and break with Chiang.
overview: This archival file from the U.S. State Department's decimal central files (Record Group 59) brings together two distinct components relating to Japan during the 1930s. The first part consists of five Form DS-46 'List of Papers' docket sheets for decimal file 894.0011 (Imperial Family - Japan), indexing communications from 1930 to 1937 regarding imperial weddings, births of imperial children (notably Crown Prince Akihito in 1933), overseas goodwill trips of imperial princes, and related diplomatic representations. The second and main part of the file is American Embassy Tokyo Despatch No. 2787, dated February 19, 1938, signed by Ambassador Joseph C. Grew, transmitting Embassy Report No. 136, 'Report on Conditions in Japan During the Month of January, 1938' (filed under 894.00 P.R./122). The 36-page report, accompanied by comprehensive schedules of all despatches and telegrams sent by the Embassy during the month, presents a detailed contemporary assessment of Japan's domestic politics, wartime economy, military operations in China, and diplomatic relations with the United States, Great Britain, the Soviet Union, Germany, Italy, and France. Key matters addressed include the assault on American diplomat John M. Allison in Nanking, Japanese military looting of neutral property, interference with Chinese maritime customs, naval expansion bills, Alaskan salmon fishing disputes, the January 11 Imperial Conference, and the Konoye Cabinet's declaration terminating relations with Chiang Kai-shek's Nationalist Government.

subfiles.about: Department of State docket sheets listing documents filed under decimal classification 894.0011 regarding the Japanese Imperial Family between 1930 and 1937.
subfiles.summary: A continuous five-page Department of State List of Papers (Form DS-46) docket register for central file 894.0011 (Imperial Family - Japan), recording incoming and outgoing correspondence from January 1930 through late 1937. Entries record document numbers, dates, correspondents, purports, and file cross-references concerning the marriage and global tour of Prince and Princess Takamatsu, Prince Chichibu's visits to China, Europe, and Canada, and official congratulations surrounding the births of imperial children, including Crown Prince Akihito in December 1933 and Prince Masahito in November 1935. The sheets also index diplomatic handling of derogatory foreign press articles and cross-references to Embassy political reports.
subfiles.title: Department of State List of Papers for Decimal File 894.0011 (Imperial Family - Japan)

subfiles.about: Covering despatch from Ambassador Joseph C. Grew transmitting the Tokyo Embassy's monthly report on conditions in Japan for January 1938.
subfiles.summary: Grew's Despatch No. 2787 transmits Embassy Report No. 136 on conditions in Japan in January 1938, copied to posts in China, Manchuria and Moscow.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 2787 from Ambassador Grew to the Secretary of State Transmitting Monthly Report No. 136

subfiles.about: Comprehensive Embassy report and attached monthly schedules detailing Japan's international relations, the Sino-Japanese conflict, domestic politics, wartime economy, and diplomatic communications during January 1938.
subfiles.summary: Embassy Report No. 136 comprehensively surveys Japanese internal and external affairs during January 1938, beginning with relations with the United States and detailing the crisis provoked when Japanese troops slapped American diplomat John M. Allison and civilian Charles Riggs in Nanking. It recounts vigorous American diplomatic protests in Tokyo over military looting of foreign property, flag desecration, interference with Chinese maritime customs administration, and illegal Japanese salmon fishing in Alaskan waters, alongside Japanese reactions to proposed U.S. naval expansion. The report details military campaigns in Shantung, the historic January 11 Imperial Conference approving a war of endurance, the rupture of tentative peace negotiations and subsequent severance of relations with Chiang Kai-shek's Nationalist Government, and the promotion of puppet autonomous regimes. International sections review friction with Great Britain over assaults on police in Shanghai and navigation rights on the Yangtze, border and fisheries disputes with the Soviet Union, German mediation efforts, and Italian and French diplomatic developments. Finally, the report examines domestic political developments, including the munitions industry mobilization, electric power state control legislation, national budget expansion, foreign trade deficits, labor union reorientation, and concludes with exhaustive schedules of all despatches and telegrams sent to Washington by the Embassy during January 1938.
subfiles.title: Report No. 136: Report on Conditions in Japan During the Month of January, 1938
